newsitem.title: GERMANY: CalPERS to target non-U.S. underperformers in 1997.
newsitem.headline: CalPERS to target non-U.S. underperformers in 1997.

text.p: The California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS), the largest U.S. pension fund, said on Monday it could draw up a list of underperfoming companies in Europe and Japan by mid-1997.

"We intend to have a more definitive programme developed by mid-1997 for the United Kingdom and France and later in 1997 for Germany and Japan," Jim Burton, CalPERS chief executive, told Reuters in an interview.

Burton said the fund's corporate governance programme in the U.S. was based on dealing with the underperformance of particular stocks and said this approach would be brought to the fund's analysis of international markets.
The $100 billion fund launched its international corporate governance programme in March to extend its practice of shareholder activism outside the United States.
CalPERS has a reputation for pushing the interests of shareholders through active involvement in the management of companies in which it holds large stakes.

But Burton was keen to reassure possible "underperformers", saying the fund was taking a cautious approach in its new international programme, and had to take time to learn and understand, before it "jumped in."
"There is nervousness because of what I think is a mischaracterisation of CalPERS in the press, that we are overly aggressive, that we are outspoken and ill informed," said Burton.
"We have made a particular effort to say we don't view short-term solutions, such as downsizing to promote the stock price in the short term, as a viable answer," said Burton.
"We would expect management to be more thoughtful and strategic and we are there to support them in that."

Burton, who is in Germany to promote investment in California, said he welcomed the growing awareness of the idea of shareholder value in the country, which is receiving increasing interest as German companies look to access more international capital.
German companies are traditionally run on a consensus model, where shareholder interests take second place to the powerful position of banks and employees.
"I am intrigued by the amount of union representation on supervisory boards," said Burton.
